title: Letters to Ephesus, Smyrna, Pergamum, and Thyatira
summary: The risen Christ speaks to four of the seven churches. Ephesus is doctrinally careful but has abandoned its first love. Smyrna is poor and slandered, and is told to be faithful unto death. Pergamum has held firm where Satan's throne is but tolerates teaching that leads to idolatry and immorality. Thyatira is growing in love and service but tolerates a false prophetess called Jezebel. Each church receives a promise for the one who overcomes.
story: In chapter 1 John saw Christ walking among seven lampstands, the seven churches, and was told to write to them. Chapters 2 and 3 carry out that command. Each message draws a feature from the vision of chapter 1 and applies it to one church's situation. These are the only parts of Revelation addressed directly to named congregations, and they anchor the visions that follow in real places and real struggles. The promises to the overcomers look ahead to the end of the book, where the tree of life, the crown, and the new name reappear.
historical:
Ephesus was the greatest city of the Roman province of Asia, a port near the mouth of the Cayster River and one of the largest cities in the eastern half of the empire. It was famous for the temple of Artemis, one of the seven wonders of the ancient world, and it also held temples of the imperial cult, including one to the Flavian emperors dedicated in the time of Domitian. Paul had worked there for more than two years (Acts 19), and Christian tradition later linked John with the city. Its harbor was steadily silting up, a slow threat to its prosperity that some commentators connect with the warning that its lampstand could be removed.

Smyrna (modern Izmir), a rich port north of Ephesus, was known for its loyalty to Rome. It built a temple to the goddess Roma as early as 195 BC and in AD 26 won the right to build a temple to the emperor Tiberius. The old city had been destroyed around 600 BC and lay in ruins for centuries before being refounded around 300 BC, a history some connect with Christ's title, the one who died and returned to life. Its bishop Polycarp was burned to death there in the mid-second century. Pergamum, inland to the north, had been the capital of the Attalid kings, whose last ruler bequeathed the kingdom to Rome in 133 BC. Its acropolis held a great altar of Zeus and temples to many gods; the city had a famous healing sanctuary of Asclepius; and in 29 BC it received the first temple in Asia to Augustus and Roma. Thyatira, southeast of Pergamum, was a smaller commercial town with many trade guilds; Lydia, the seller of purple cloth whom Paul met at Philippi, came from there (Acts 16:14).
cultural:
The pressures in these letters come largely from ordinary economic and civic life. Trade guilds, such as those attested at Thyatira for wool workers, dyers, leather workers, and bronze smiths, held regular banquets in honor of patron gods, where meat sacrificed to idols was served and sexual immorality was not unusual. A Christian craftsman who refused to take part could lose his business connections. The teaching of Balaam and of Jezebel, which led people to eat food sacrificed to idols and commit sexual immorality (verses 14 and 20), likely offered a way to stay in that world by treating such participation as harmless. Balaam, in Numbers 25 and 31, was remembered for leading Israel into idolatry and immorality at Peor; Jezebel, Ahab's queen, promoted Baal worship in Israel (1 Kings 16 and 21). The Nicolaitans (verses 6 and 15) are otherwise unknown; Irenaeus linked them with Nicolas of Acts 6:5, but that connection is uncertain.

The phrase where the throne of Satan sits (verse 13) has been explained several ways: the great altar of Zeus, the serpent symbol of Asclepius, the city's role as a center of emperor worship, or the fact that the Roman governor held court there with power over life and death. The slander from those who claim to be Jews (verse 9) reflects local conflicts in which Christians, no longer seen as part of the synagogue, lost the legal protection that Judaism enjoyed. The white stone (verse 17) is also debated; white stones were used as votes of acquittal in courts and as tokens of admission to feasts, and either could fit.
literary: Each of the seven messages follows a similar pattern. It opens with the command to write to the angel of the church, then a title of Christ drawn from chapter 1. Next comes I know, followed by praise, then (in most) a rebuke introduced by but I have this against you, a call to repent, a warning, and a promise to the one who overcomes. Each ends with the refrain He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches, which makes clear that every church was meant to hear every message. In the first three letters the refrain comes before the promise; from Thyatira on it comes after. The promises draw on the whole biblical story: the tree of life from Eden, manna from the wilderness, rule over the nations from Psalm 2, and the morning star.

outline.t: Ephesus: faithful doctrine, lost first love
Smyrna: poor but rich, faithful unto death

doctrines.note: Christ knows each congregation intimately, its deeds, its suffering, and its compromises. The church belongs to him, and he both commends and corrects it.
Repent occurs repeatedly in the chapter. Even churches under pressure are called to turn from compromise and lost love, and even Jezebel was given time to repent (verse 21).
The false teachers at Pergamum and Thyatira made room for eating food sacrificed to idols and for sexual immorality. Idolatry here is practical and social, bound up with trade and civic life.
Smyrna receives no rebuke, only encouragement to be faithful unto death. Suffering is limited (ten days) and known to Christ, and it is not the last word: the crown of life is.

words.note: Nikao, to conquer or overcome, the word behind every closing promise. In Revelation believers conquer not by force but as the Lamb did, through faithful witness even to death (12:11). The word would have evoked Nike, the goddess of victory, whose images were common in these cities.

Stephanos, crown or wreath, the garland given to victors in athletic games or worn at festivals, not a royal diadem. Smyrna was proud of its games and its civic crowns. Christ promises the faithful the crown of life, the victor's reward that no city could give.

Metanoeo, to repent, to change one's mind and direction. It occurs six times in this chapter, addressed to Ephesus, Pergamum, and Thyatira. Christ's words are not only judgment but invitation: he calls for repentance before he comes to judge.

christ: Each letter begins with a title of Christ taken from the vision of chapter 1, fitted to the church's need. To Ephesus he is the one who walks among the lampstands, present in the church and able to remove it. To suffering Smyrna he is the First and the Last, who died and came to life, the answer to their fear of death. To Pergamum he holds the sharp two-edged sword, the word that judges and the authority that outranks Rome's. To Thyatira he is the Son of God with eyes like fire and feet like bronze, who searches minds and hearts. He knows each church, promises rewards that echo the whole Bible's story, and shares his own authority from the Father with those who overcome (verses 26-27, drawing on Psalm 2).

hard.q: What does synagogue of Satan mean, and hasn't such language fueled hatred of Jewish people?
hard.a:
The phrase in verse 9 (and in 3:9) is among the hardest in Revelation, and it must be handled carefully. It does not describe the Jewish people as a whole. John himself was Jewish, the book is saturated with Israel's Scriptures, and the new Jerusalem bears the names of the twelve tribes. The phrase addresses a local conflict in Smyrna in which some members of a synagogue were slandering Christians, perhaps denouncing them to Roman authorities, at a time when Christians were being pushed out of the protection given to Judaism. John's charge is that by joining in persecution they were acting as the accuser (the meaning of Satan) and so were not living as true Jews in the sense of faithful Israel. Paul uses similar inside language in Romans 2:28-29.

It is also true that phrases like this were later torn from their setting and used by Christians to justify contempt and violence against Jews, a history the church has rightly confessed and repented of. Reading the verse faithfully means reading it as the book's first hearers would have: as a word about particular accusers in one city, not a verdict on a people.

questions: Ephesus was careful about doctrine but had left its first love. How can a church or a person be right and yet lose love?
Smyrna is poor but called rich. What would it look like to measure your life by Christ's account rather than by what your city values?
The false teaching at Pergamum and Thyatira made compromise seem harmless. Where are you tempted to call a small accommodation to idolatry just being practical?
